query: For an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating susceptible to progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its creep resistance? Specify the governing factor and rationale, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, the operating boundaries under sustained stress, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the coherency and relative volume fraction of the FCC/BCC phase boundaries in the as-deposited dual-phase high-entropy alloy coating enhances creep resistance by impeding dislocation motion during sustained loading.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-deposited dual-phase high-entropy alloy protective coating possessing interspersed FCC and BCC microstructural constituents with varying interface coherency.
generation.intervention: Tailor the microstructure via controlled deposition and annealing protocols to systematically vary the relative volume fractions and interface coherency between the FCC and BCC phases.
generation.conditions: Sustained creep loading conditions at temperatures and stresses relevant to progressive plastic deformation, where steady-state creep behavior can be measured.
generation.structural_mediator: The coherency and density of FCC/BCC phase boundaries, which act as obstacles to dislocation movement.
generation.mechanism: Coherent phase boundaries increase local dislocation pile-up and hinder dislocation climb, thereby slowing creep deformation. This barrier effect is enhanced when the FCC phase fraction and interface coherency are maximized.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with higher FCC/BCC interface coherency and increased FCC phase fraction will exhibit lower creep strain rates and delayed onset of steady-state deformation compared to a baseline microstructure with lower interphase coherency.
generation.baseline: The original as-deposited coating microstructure with its inherent mix of FCC and BCC phases and less coherent phase boundaries.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold in the creep regime under continuous loading at elevated temperatures where dislocation climb and plastic deformation are operative.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative reduction in creep rate is uncertain due to complexities in dislocation–interface interactions; however, a clear trend correlating interphase coherence with creep resistance is anticipated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple sets of the high-entropy alloy coating using identical deposition methods but vary the post-deposition annealing parameters to produce a systematic gradient in FCC/BCC phase fraction and interface coherency. Subject each set to identical sustained creep loading conditions at a controlled elevated temperature and monitor deformation over time.
measurements: Creep strain rate and total strain accumulation over a fixed duration under constant load.
Microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM, SEM) to quantify FCC/BCC volume fractions and interface coherency.
Dislocation density and interaction mapping near phase boundaries using high-resolution imaging techniques.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no statistically significant correlation is found between increased FCC/BCC interface coherency (or higher FCC phase fraction) and improved creep resistance (i.e., reduced creep strain rate or delayed steady-state creep) compared to the baseline sample, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

Abstract A NbMoTaWVTi refractory high entropy alloy (HEA) has been successfully synthesized by mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS). The microstructure and mechanical properties of this alloy are investigated. It is observed that only two types of body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solutions are formed in the powders after ball milling for 40 h. However, a new face-centered cubic (FCC) precipitated phase is observed in the BCC matrix of bulk material consolidated by SPS. The FCC precipitated phase is identified as TiO, due to the introduction of O during the preparing process of HEA. The compressive yield strength, fracture strength, and total fracture strain of the consolidated bulk HEA are 2709 MPa, 3115 MPa, and 11.4%, respectively. The excellent mechanical properties can be attributed to solid solution strengthening and grain boundary strengthening of the fine-grained BCC matrix, as well as the precipitation strengthening owing to the formation of TiO particles. Keywords: refractory high entropy alloy, microstructure, mechanical properties

Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe. decision.trend: Early research on high-entropy alloys focused on single‐phase mechanisms such as dislocation climb and grain-boundary sliding under dynamic loading conditions. As work progressed, studies began to incorporate processing routes (e.g., HPHT treatment, mechanical alloying, spark plasma sintering) to deliberately develop dual‐phase microstructures (FCC combined with variants of BCC/B2) with the aim of balancing strength and ductility. These investigations revealed that the interface between different phases plays a role in impeding dislocation motion and enhancing macroscopic mechanical behavior. However, none of the earlier studies definitively isolated the reinforcement effect of FCC/BCC phase boundaries under sustained, creep loading.
decision.unsolved: What remains unclear is the precise mechanistic contribution of the FCC/BCC phase boundaries in arresting dislocation motion under continuous loading and how variations in phase fraction and interface coherency govern the observed creep resistance.
decision.lever: Systematically modulate the relative volume fractions and interface coherency of the FCC and BCC phases (via tailored deposition/annealing protocols) to isolate their effect on creep behavior
decision.why: Following the trend that dual-phase interactions may be key to enhanced performance, the next logical experiment is a controlled comparison where only the microstructural attributes (phase fraction and interface structures) are varied. This would directly test if improved interface coherence correlates with reduced creep deformation, thereby addressing the identified gap and providing a clear falsification criterion if no such correlation is observed under the defined creep regime.
